implementation_notes: The standard library already contains the guard loop: condition_variable::wait(lock, pred) is specified as while (!pred()) wait(lock), so spurious wake-ups need no attention in application code, and the condition variable's unlock/notify ordering cannot lose a signal issued after the wait began. A condition variable may only ever be used with one mutex, which is why the mutex and the condition belong to the same guarded object; notify_one suits interchangeable waiters, notify_all the multi-predicate case, and notifying after releasing the lock avoids waking a thread that would immediately block on the mutex again. Reach for std::atomic::wait when the guard is a single word in lock-free code, and for std::future/std::promise or a channel when the caller is waiting for one specific result rather than for shared state.
pitfalls: condition_variable is bound to one mutex: waiting on it with a second mutex is undefined behaviour, so keep the pair private to the guarded object.
Destroying a condition variable (or the mutex) while a thread is still blocked on it is undefined behaviour; stop and join waiters before teardown.
A predicate that reads state not protected by the same mutex races even though the wait itself is correct - publish the guarded fields under that mutex or through an atomic.

variants.name: std::atomic<T>::wait / notify_one (C++20)
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 added waiting to atomics: atomic<T>::wait(old) blocks until the value representation differs from old and is woken by notify_one/notify_all, and cppreference notes the guarantee that the call returns only if the value actually changed - spurious unblocks are internal. That makes a single-word guard (a sequence counter, a state enum, a published index) expressible without a mutex, which is useful for handoff counters in lock-free pipelines; compound state still needs a mutex or an immutable snapshot published through the atomic, and the ABA problem must be avoided by waiting on a monotonically changing value.
pitfalls: Waiting on a flag that can flip back (the ABA problem) may never unblock: wait on a monotonically changing counter instead.
The atomic only orders itself: the payload must be published with release/acquire semantics or the consumer may see an updated counter with stale data.
